title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
In this example, we look at how to select the walls of an arbitrarily shaped cavity in mofography.
This methodology is very useful: - For computing the stress on a wall, and you need to define a plane or a mesh or select atoms close to a wall - The cage wall doesn’t have to be flat - It doesn’t have to align with any common cell directions (a, b, c, ab, bc, ca, abc etc.)
This may get complicated - The shape of the cage may not be well defined in some materials. May not be able to break it down into distinct walls - Picking atoms near a wall using the cell list sometimes causes segmentation fault if no bonds can be detected, in this case pick the atoms and compute bonds manually without the cell list.

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
How ?
This is a simple mesh segmentation using the coordinates and normals of parts of isosurface mesh. This is the same methodology as detecting the limbs vs the body vs head of a 3D mesh of an animal.

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
section: Create isosurface mesh and Select Cavity
text:
Create isosurface mesh and Select Cavity
We carve out an isosurface mesh and then select the cages of insterest using their region labels. For example if we visualize what we have so far, and say we want to select the cavity numbered in ‘select’
Here’s all the cages visualized:

Visualize

import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px

cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Plotly

isosurface_trace = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid.compute(
), isovalue=2.5, ase_atoms=mat_updated, region_labels=regions, cscale=cscale, opacity=1)
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_updated)
fig = go.Figure(data=[isosurface_trace]).update(layout=mgr.white_layout)
fig.show()
# frame_trace = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated)

                                                




Create submesh
We are going to use the region labels to select the vertices that form cavity numberd in select from the overall isosurface

from scipy.interpolate import RegularGridInterpolator as RGI
import trimesh, numpy as np
from ase.geometry import complete_cell

# select this regions
select=[18] 

# cell matrix
cell = complete_cell(mat_atoms.get_cell())

# isosurfae of all cavities at 2 angstroms
isomesh = mgr.get_isosurface_mesh(dgrid.compute(), 2,cell)

# vertices and faces of the isosurface in fractional coordinates
verts, faces = isomesh.vertices, isomesh.faces
verts = mgr.get_fractional_coordinates(verts, mat_atoms)

# interpolator for region labels
rl = mgr.interpolate_labels(regions)

# pick faces for which the region labels match
select_these_faces = np.where(np.all(np.isin(rl(verts[faces]), select, assume_unique=False), axis=1))

# make a submesh using the selected faces
submesh = isomesh.submesh(select_these_faces, append=True).subdivide()



Visualize submesh
Let’s plot and see if we have the correct submesh.

cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_updated)
submesh_trace = mgr.plot_mesh(
    [submesh], stylize=True, name='submesh for regions {}'.format(select))
go.Figure(data=[cell_trace, submesh_trace]).update(layout=mgr.white_layout).show()

                                                


this cage looks like a truncated octahedron, where the faces are curved instead of flat triagles. It has 12 faces, and 6 windows. We want to detect and distinguish the 12 faces.


Segment Mesh
We are going to use agglomerative clustering to group the vertices of the above mesh into different faces. At each vertex, we have 6 values (features), 3 positions and 3 direction cosines for the normal.
Note: We can use PCA, t-SNE, UMAP etc. to reduce the dimensionality, but here we need not, since we have only 6 features.

# Create a scaled set of features for better clustering
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering 
X = np.hstack((submesh.vertices, submesh.vertex_normals))
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# # Use PCA
# from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
# X_pca = PCA(n_components=5).fit_transform(X_scaled)


# from sklearn.manifold import TSNE 
# X = TSNE(n_components=3).fit_transform(X)

# agglomerative clustering, the distance threshold doesn't matter that much.
clst = AgglomerativeClustering(linkage='single',distance_threshold=0.25, n_clusters=None)
clst.fit(X)
labels = clst.labels_

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
Note:
As we will see shortly, one natural drawback is the clustering algorithm gets confused at the ridges between two faces, since the normals can fluctuate a lot close to the edge where they become discontinuous. But, we can easily eliminate these ridge pixels, since they will few in number in between.

Eliminate Ridge clusters
These clusters will have far too few points to be a face. Let’s elimiate them.


# counts in each cluster
_, counts = np.unique(labels, return_counts=True)

# remove clusters with les than 100 points,
counts_cutoff=100
keep_these_labels = np.unique(labels)[np.where(np.array(counts)>counts_cutoff)]


# grab vertices corresponding to valid clusters
vertex_selections = [submesh.vertices[np.where(labels==l)] for l in keep_these_labels]

# get centroids for valid clusters
cage_wall_centroids = np.array([np.mean(s,axis=0) for s in vertex_selections])

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
Visualize clustering
Let’s visualize the results of our clustering.

Relabel
But first let’s relabel the vertices from 0 to n-1, where n is the number of valid clusters. All the points belonging to invalid clusters are labeled -1. We are going to call these labels unique_colorvals, as we will be using them for plotting

# relabel as described above
colorvals = [l if l in keep_these_labels else -1 for l in labels]
_,unique_colorvals = np.unique(colorvals, return_inverse=True)




Plot the results
Now we can apply a colorscale using matplotlib and visualize the results using mofography (plotly, basically).



# apply colormap to get a list of colors and add that to the mesh
import matplotlib as mpl 
colors = mpl.cm.get_cmap('tab20c')(unique_colorvals)
colors[:, :-1] = (colors[:, :-1]*255).astype(int)
submesh.visual.vertex_colors=colors
submesh_trace = mgr.plot_mesh(
    [submesh], hovertext=np.array(unique_colorvals).astype(str), stylize=True, name='submesh for region {}'.format(select[0]))
go.Figure(data=submesh_trace).update(layout=mgr.white_layout).show()

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
Pick framework atoms
Now that we have the centroids of the walls, we can pick atoms from the unit cell that are close to one or more of the centroids very easily using the AABB cell list from freud that is already implementd in mofography. In this example we are simply selecting all atoms within ‘r_max’ distance using ‘ball’ query, instead you may also choose n_neighbors using a ‘nearest’ query.

aabb=mgr.AABB_on_atoms(mat_atoms)
ab_r = aabb.query(cage_wall_centroids, query_args=dict(mode='ball',  r_max=5))
ab_r_nl = ab_r.toNeighborList(sort_by_distance=True)
pick_these_atoms = ab_r_nl.point_indices

title: Region Adjacency Graph (RAG) or the Pore Graph
text:
In this tutorial, we explain, compute and analyze the region adjacency graph of our region segmentation. RAG is not a new concept, in fact, it has been recently implemented in scikit-image RAG skimage. However, we build it with some modifications.
RAG is simply a graph of the touching regions in an image. In our case, the nodes of the graph represent the pockets the position of the node can be set at the local maxima (or the centroid) of the region. The edges represent an actual connection in the cavities, where one pore is connected to another through a pore window. Hence, in this context the terms RAG and pore graph are used interchangeably. Pore graph is very useful, because:
In this tutorial, we will be relying on all the tutorials up to the ‘Applying PBC’ tutorial. Although, not all of them are required to construct the pore graph, all the additional information we will add to the pore graph will be based on the previous tutorials. Hence, it is recommended to go through all the tutorials before this one. Let’s get up to speed, as before, we will not be explaning the build-up steps in detail.

title: Region Adjacency Graph (RAG) or the Pore Graph
section: Constructing the Region Adjacency Graph (RAG) or the Pore Graph
text:
Constructing the Region Adjacency Graph (RAG) or the Pore Graph
There are a few ways in mofography to generate the pore graph from what we have so far. Perhaps the easiest option is to use the get_rag_from_regions_and_grid function. It also needs the ASE atoms object, the maxima maybe provided as an argument if you’d like to fix the locations of the node manually or to speed up the calculations a little bit. If not provided, the local maxima of the distance grid will be computed on the fly as in the region segmentation step.
However, this is not the recommended option, because it tends to fail when there is only one region in the box, which is quite common in nanoporous materials due to PBC. Hence, the slower robust option is to compute the connections first and then compute the RAG from the connections list. ‘connections’ is a list that contains information about the connections between regions in the material and the corresponding pore windows. Please refer to the window detection tutorial for detailed explanation and examples.
Let’s try make the RAG both ways, for IRMOF-1, CuBTC etc, both approaches give same results.
Note: that you shouldn’t use the regions_pbc instead of regions here, because the number of unique regions will not match the number of maxima in the box, and will result in an error. We will the PBC information as an additional property to the pore graph in the next step.

Option 1: Using the get_rag_from_regions_and_grid function (NOT RECOMMENDED)

rag = mgr.get_rag_from_regions_and_grid(regions, dgrid.compute(), mat_atoms, maxima)



Option 2: Compute connections first and then compute the RAG from the connections list (RECOMMENDED)
Please refer to the window detection tutorial for detailed explanation and examples on the connections list.


connections = mgr.connections_from_regions_and_dgrid(regions, dgrid.compute(), maxima, mat_atoms)

rag = mgr.rag_from_connections(connections, maxima)
#* let's add some properties to the RAG
shape = dgrid.shape
#* add the maxima to the rag
rag = mgr.add_maxima_to_rag(rag, maxima, maxima_radii, shape, mat_atoms)
#* add the region props from skiamge
# props = mgr.get_region_props_for_regions(regions)
# rag = mgr.add_props_to_rag(rag, props)

This is a networkx style graph object, hence all the networkx functions to obtain attributes or to manipulate the graph are available. For example, to get the nodes and edges of the graph use:

import networkx as nx 

rag.nodes(), rag.edges()

It takes an ase atoms object and returns a networkx graph object with the nodes and edges corresponding to the atoms and bonds in the atoms object.
The function also takes two optional arguments:

node_props_dict: A dictionary of node properties. The keys are the names of the properties and the values are the values of the properties. The values should be a list of the same length as the number of atoms in the atoms object.
edge_props_dict: A dictionary of edge properties. The keys are the names of the properties and the values are the values of the properties. The values should be a list of the same length as the number of bonds in the atoms object.

If the node_props_dict or edge_props_dict are not provided, the function will use the default set of properties.

title: regions_from_dgrid
text:
compute.regions_from_dgrid(dgrid, mask_thickness=1, h=0.2, min_distance=2, compactness=0)
The function regions_from_dgrid takes a density grid as input and identifies regions based on local maxima, with options for adjusting parameters like mask thickness and compactness.











Name
Type
Description
Default




dgrid

The dgrid parameter is a 2D array representing the input data grid. It is used in the function to perform calculations and identify regions based on the data values in the grid
required


mask_thickness

The mask_thickness parameter in the regions_from_dgrid function determines the thickness of the mask used in the watershed segmentation algorithm. It is used to create a mask where regions with values greater than the mask_thickness are considered as markers for segmentation. Increasing the mask_thickness value, defaults to 1 (optional)
1


h

The h parameter in the regions_from_dgrid function is used to specify the height threshold for detecting local maxima in the input dgrid array. It is used in the extrema.h_maxima function to find the local maxima points based on the specified height
0.2


min_distance

The min_distance parameter in the regions_from_dgrid function specifies the minimum distance between peaks in the peak_local_max function. This is a wrapper for the MOFDB API, which is explained here:https://mof.tech.northwestern.edu/api It takes in a url, parameters, headers, number of pages and a path to the mofography repository and returns a pandas dataframe of the data.
The function is asynchronous and uses the aiohttp library to make multiple requests to the MOFDB API.











Name
Type
Description
Default




url

The url of the MOF database, defaults to https://mof.tech.northwestern.edu/mofs/#.json (optional)
'https://mof.tech.northwestern.edu/mofs/#.json'


params

a dictionary of parameters to be passed to the url. The default parameters are: {‘vf_min’: 0.1, ‘vf_max’: 1.0, ‘database’:‘IZA’,‘page’:1}
{'vf_min': 0.1, 'vf_max': 1.0, 'database': 'IZA', 'page': 1}


headers

This is the headers that you want to pass to the MOFDB API. The default is to get the loading and pressure data
{'loading': 'cm3(STP)/cm3', 'pressure': 'bar'}


npages

number of pages to be scraped. If None, then the number of pages is determined by the function to return all the pages
None


limit

maximum number of pages allowed in the query (no need to change this one unless overflow )
1000









Type
Description





A dataframe with the results of the query.

title: dgrid_from_atoms_cpu
text:
compute.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(ase_atoms, radii=None, spacing=0.25, block_size=50000, n_neighbors=10, probe_radius=0, precompute=True)
This function generates a distance grid over atoms using Dask arrays and pandas, with an option to precompute the grid.











Name
Type
Description
Default




ase_atoms

The ase_atoms parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms_cpu function is expected to be an ASE Atoms object, which represents a collection of atoms and their positions in space. This object typically contains information about the atomic species, positions, and unit cell of a molecular system
required


radii

The radii parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms_cpu function is used to specify the atomic radii for the atoms in the input ase_atoms object. If the radii parameter is not provided by the user, a default set of van der Waals radii
None


spacing

The spacing parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms_cpu function represents the distance between grid points in the mesh grid that is created over the atoms. It determines how finely the grid is sampled in space. A smaller spacing value will result in a denser grid with more grid points, while
0.25


block_size

The block_size parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms_cpu function is used to specify the size of each block when processing the grid points. It determines how the grid points are divided into smaller blocks for computation. A larger block size can lead to better performance in terms of memory usage and, defaults to 50000 (optional)
50000


n_neighbors

The n_neighbors parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms_cpu function represents the number of nearest neighbors to consider when computing the distance grid. It is used in the calculation of the distance grid based on the provided atoms and radii. Increasing the n_neighbors value will result in a, defaults to 10 (optional)
10


probe_radius

The probe_radius parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms_cpu function represents the radius of the probe used for computing the distance grid. It is used in conjunction with the atomic radii to determine the distance between atoms and the grid points. The probe radius helps in defining the spatial constraints for, defaults to 0 (optional)
0


precompute

The precompute parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms_cpu function determines whether the computation of the distance grid should be immediately executed and the final result returned (precompute=True), or if a lazy Dask array representing the computation should be returned without executing it (precompute=False), defaults to True (optional)
True













Type
Description





The function dgrid_from_atoms_cpu returns the computed distance grid. If precompute is set to True, it returns the computed distance grid as a Dask array. If precompute is set to False, it returns the Dask array without computing it, allowing for further computations to be performed later.

title: add_psd_to_rag
text:
compute.add_psd_to_rag(G, region_props, bins, ase_atoms, shape)

This function takes a graph, a list of region properties, a list of bins, an ase atoms object, and a shape, and adds the psd to the graph.

For each region, we calculate the distances between the centroid and the coordinates.
Then we calculate the histogram of the distances.
Then we calculate the bin centers.
Then we add the bin centers and the histogram to the graph.
Then we return the graph.
Note that these distance histograms or centroids do not account for periodic boundary conditions. To include periodic boundary conditions, use the add_psd_to_rag_with_pbc function.

compute.add_maxima_to_rag(G, maxima, maxima_radii, shape, ase_atoms)

This function takes a graph, a list of maxima, a list of maxima radii, a shape, and an ase_atoms object and adds the maxima and maxima radii to the graph.

Let’s look at the function in more detail.
The first thing we do is import the find_coord_from_indices function from the helper module.
Next, we check to make sure that the number of nodes in the graph is equal to the number of maxima. If not, we raise a ValueError.
If the number of nodes in the graph is equal to the number of maxima, we loop through the nodes and maxima and add the maxima indices, cartesian coordinates and maxima radii to the graph.

Adds cluster information to a region adjacency graph (RAG) by calculating the Jensen-Shannon distance between two histograms of distances.
Args: rag (networkx.Graph): the RAG graph props (list): list of properties of each region in the RAG pbc_groups (list): list of groups of regions with periodic boundary conditions (PBC) ase_atoms (ase.Atoms): ASE atoms object shape (tuple): shape of the region use_pbc (bool): whether to use PBC or not js_threshold (float): the threshold for the Jensen-Shannon distance
Returns: networkx.Graph: the RAG with cluster information added under keys ‘cluster_geom_pbc’ or ‘cluster_geom_nopbc’ depending on whether ‘use_pbc’ is True or False

title: add_centroids_to_rag_with_pbc
text:
compute.add_centroids_to_rag_with_pbc(rag, props, pbc_groups, ase_atoms, shape)

For each group of nodes that are connected by periodic boundary conditions, find the centroid of the group and add it to the graph as a node attribute.

The function takes in a graph, a list of properties, a list of groups of nodes that are connected by periodic boundary conditions, an ASE atoms object, and the shape of the image.
The function first makes a copy of the graph. Then, it loops through each group of nodes that are connected by periodic boundary conditions. For each group, it finds the indices of the properties that correspond to the nodes in the group. If there is more than one node in the group, it finds the centroid of the group by taking the circular mean of the coordinates of the nodes in the group. If there is only one node in the group, it finds the centroid of the node by taking the mean of the coordinates of the node. Finally, it adds the centroid of the group

title: Quick Clustering Workflow
text: This notebook demonstrates a quick clustering workflow used in detecting the different types of pockets in a nanoporouse material. It uses a collection of default parameters and may not work perfectly for all materials. But, it is a good starting point for tuning. The steps used in this workflow are: - Compute the grid - Compute the local maxima in the grid - Compute region segmentation - Apply periodic boundary conditions - Detect connectivity and construct a pore graph - Add some basic properties to the nodes of the pore graph - Make figures with all the information

title: Detecting Types of Pockets
text:
In this tutorial, we will learn the details on how to how to detect the different tyupes of pockets in am aterial using unsupervised machine learning. For this, we will realy on everything up to the region adjacency graph that we have seen in earlier tutorials. So, if you haven’t tried thos out please go back check those out first, in order to make sense out of this tutorial. You may think of this tutorial as an under-the-hood explanation of the Quick Cluster notebook, among the earlier tutorials.
The steps needed to detect the different types of pockets are:
Since, we have already worked up to the region adjacency graph (RAG) so far, we will quickly run through the steps until then without explanation.

title: Detecting Types of Pockets
text:
Assigning cavity level features
Now we we can annotate each node of the RAG with cavity level features. We can simply use purely geometric, distance based features to represent each pocket. Core set of features built-in to mofography is the pocket size distribution. The pocket size distribution is simply a normalized histogram of the distances of all the points in a region to the centroid of the region. The effect of periodic boundary conditions can be included to the features as follows. For each PBC group (the list of pockets that are connected by periodic boundary conditions), the shortest distance (with PBC) to the periodic centroid is histogrammed. The periodic centroid of a PBC group, is the centroid of a all the points in all the regions in that list, averaged in 3D cyclic coordinates. As a result, the histogram features of given type of cavity that is fully inside a unit cell, and that is split across periodic boundaries will be the same, as long as PBC is accounted for correctly. We can add the pocket size distribution to the RAG as follows after choosing a histogram range that works well in most cases.

import numpy as np
bins = np.linspace(0,30,50)
rag = mgr.add_psd_to_rag_with_pbc(rag, props, pbc_groups, bins, mat_atoms, regions.shape)

title: Detecting Types of Pockets
text:
Visualizing the results
The best way to visualize the clustering is to color the distance isosurface with the cluster number. We can do this using the mofography. But first we have turn this clustering information into a 3D grid wherer each voxel is labeled wit hthe cluster number. For this we take the 3D grid of regions, find the corresponding PBC group number and map the cluster number on to the PBC group. We can do this using the mofography function clustering_grid_from_regions as follows.

regions_clusters = mgr.clustering_grid_from_regions(regions, rag, cluster_key='cluster_geom_pbc')


np.unique(regions_clusters)

As you can see, the two pocket types are indicated by color. Now, it might seem counterintuitive initially, that there are two types of pockets in IRMOF-1, but this is true. This happens because of the orientation of the aromatic rings on the BDC linkers. We can look at the pocket size distribution of each PBC group to see the difference. We can do this using the mofography function pocket_size_distribution as follows. Plotting the features is also quite useful for debugging if the clustering seems wrong.

Plotting the features
Let’s plot the pocket size distribution features and color them by the cluster number.

As you can see there are two disntinct type of pockets, detected by mofography in IRMOF-1


Adjusting the threshold
In the clustering function there is an option to adjust the Jensen SHannon distance threshold, by default it is set to 0.15, meaning if the pockets are more than 15% different, then they are considered different. You may change that for your use case, for example, in the case of IRMOF-1 if we increase that value substantially, you’ll see only one type of pocket detected.

rag = mgr.add_clustering_to_rag_geometry_js(rag, props, pbc_groups, mat_atoms, dgrid.shape, js_threshold=0.5) # 50% is way too high, but just for the sake of the example

print('Unique clusters:', np.unique(regions_clusters))

title: Detecting Types of Pockets
text:
Pockets detection using energy
As mentioned earlier, one great flexibility of graphs is that we can use whatever features we want to describe each node. In mofography, there is also an option to detect pocket types using simple VdW energy calculations using UFF force field and helium probe, instead of geometric features. Sometimes this can be more useful, especially if you are already calculating the energy grid for something else. Also, the natural shape of Lennard-Jones potential makes it more sensitive close to the framework and less sensitive far away, which is good for describing pocket shape.

rag = mgr.add_clustering_to_rag_energy_js(rag, regions, energy_interpolator=None, js_threshold=0.15, ase_atoms=mat_atoms, pbc_groups = pbc_groups) # energy histograms are way more sensitive. 5% is good default choice

If you want, you can compute the energy grid first, make an interpolator and then pass that along to speed up the process substantially (otherwise it will compute the energy at a bunch of sampled points for each region). We can do another tutorial on energy grid calculation, force fields and probes, if there is interest.

egrid = mgr.egrid_from_atoms2(mat_atoms, spacing=0.5, probe_symbol='He').compute()
einterpolator = mgr.interpolate_dgrid(egrid) # we can use the same interpolator as that for the distance grid, because at the end of the day, it's just a 3D array and we are interpolating in fractional coordinates

rag = mgr.add_clustering_to_rag_energy_js(rag, regions, energy_interpolator=einterpolator, js_threshold=0.15, pbc_groups = pbc_groups) # no need for ase_atoms, because we already have the energy interpolator 


Visualize the results
Let’s visualize the results and plot the energy histogram features.


regions_clusters = mgr.clustering_grid_from_regions(regions, rag, cluster_key='cluster_energy_pbc')
print('Unique clusters:', np.unique(regions_clusters))
import plotly.express as px 
import plotly.graph_objects as go
cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel

isosurface_pbc = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid.compute(), stylize=True, isovalue=1.75, region_labels=regions_pbc, ase_atoms=mat_atoms, name='pbc',  opacity=1, cscale=cscale )
isosurface_clusters = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid.compute(), stylize=True, isovalue=1.75, region_labels=regions_clusters, name='pocket_types', ase_atoms=mat_atoms, opacity=1, cscale=cscale)
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_atoms)
frame_trace = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated, stylize=True)
fig = go.Figure(data=[isosurface_segmentation, isosurface_pbc, isosurface_clusters, cell_trace, *frame_trace])

Where to next?
We are almost at the end of the Basic Tutorials. One thing that we can do with the knowledge of the pockets is to detect the different types of channels present in the material. What we consider as a channel and how we can use some ideas from Graph theory to detect and distinguish them in practice is in the Detecting Paths tutorial.
Also, with your current mastery of the Basic Tutorials, all of the Advanced Tutorials should be quite accessible to you. So, feel free to jump there as well.

title: Compute percolation paths
text:
In this tutorial, we illustrate how to compute percolation paths in a crystalline material using mofography. Computing percolation is important for a variety of applications including, - calculating the Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) of a material - determining the accessibility of a pocket, subject to a certain probe size - diffusion related applications.
However, computing percolation paths is highly non-trivial in periodic materials. There is quite a bit of existing theory on doing this using grids, however, mofography already abstracts this grid into a pore graph, which means we can use path finding on graphs to compute percolation paths. This will be orders of magnitude faster than grid-based methods. However, the the number of all possible paths between a pair of nodes increases exponentially with the number of nodes, hence, this approach alone is greatly limiting. Hence, mofography uses a combination of two types of pathfinding algorithms as an approximation to find all the relevant paths for most applications. By relevant, we mean that paths that are the shortest in most cases, geometrically unique basis based on the types of pockets they connect, and the one that gives us the pore limiting dia. In a nutshell, - For small unit cells, all simple paths between all pairs of nodes on the opposite faces of the unit cell will give us the percolation paths. - For larger unit cells, we use a combination of Dijkstra’s algorithm to find the shortest paths (which are usually the straight channel paths), usually contain the PLD. - Note that when we compute paths in any direction, say, ‘a’, we included the periodic connectivity in the other two directions, ‘b’ and ‘c’ to ensure that we are not missing any paths that are periodic in the other two directions. While looking for percolation in one direction, the molecules are allowed to go out of the unit cell in the other two directions, and then come back in. - We also need keep track of the internal and periodic windows along each of the paths, as these are central to determining the accessibility of the pockets.

Contents of this tutorial

Compute percolation paths
Now we have everything needed to compute the percolation paths. If anything up to this point is unclear, please refer to the basic tutorials. Ok, in the code below, you’ll notice the path_jump_cutoff parameter, this one limits the maximum length (number of edges) of the paths detected by the all possible paths part of the code. title: Compute percolation paths
text:
Conclusion
In this tutorial, we illustrated how to compute percolation paths in a crystalline material using mofography. We also illustrated how to iteratively determine the percolation paths and the Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) for a given material if the current mask_thickness is not enough to find any paths. We also showed how to view them as a DataFrame, find unique paths and plot them on the structure for a better understanding.

title: Learn MOFography 🧐
text:

title: Installation
text:
Warning



Currently, mofography works only with numpy == 1.23.*. We are working on making it compatible with the latest versions of numpy.



Install dependencies, Add path and Use. ⏩
You can simply try out mofography after installing just the dependencies. In fact, I would recommend this approach, since mofography is still in active development






Caution



MOFography has been tested with Python 3.9, it should work with other version of python, but, if you do encounter any issues, please let us know by opening an issue. Hence, feel free to create a new Python 3.9 environment for this package like this before using
conda create -n mgr_env python=3.9
conda activate mgr_env



Install the dependencies using conda or pip. You may create a new conda environment with python 3.9 for this, but it is not necessary.



Install Dependencies using Conda






Note



Note: In all the steps below, feel free to replace conda with mamba, as it is much faster at resolving dependencies and installing packages. To install mamba use conda install -c conda-forge -n base mamba


conda create -n mgr_env python=3.9
conda activate mgr_env
conda install -c conda-forge pymatgen ase dask dask-jobqueue networkx scikit-image tqdm aiohttp icecream sparse scikit-learn rich trimesh pyvista plotly furl requests freud cupy


Install Dependencies using Pip
if you’d like to install these dependencies using pip, the name of the freud package is freud-analysis so use this command instead
pip install pymatgen ase dask dask-jobqueue networkx scikit-image tqdm aiohttp icecream sparse scikit-learn rich trimesh pyvista plotly furl requests freud-analysis cupy






Note



Note: If you are using a GPU, you can install the cupy package, which is a GPU-accelerated version of numpy. This will speed up the calculations significantly. If you don’t have a GPU, you can exclude cupy from the list of dependencies.j




Clone the repo 🎎

Clone the repo Click on the green Code button and download the zip file. Unzip the file to get the repo folder, the path to which we can add and use. Alternatively, if you are using git, you may instead clone the repo using the following command from your terminal with git installed

git clone https://github.com/arung-northwestern/mofography.git .

Update if need be 🔄

If you already have a cloned repo, pull the latest changes, since the package is being updated frequently

cd mofography
git pull



Add path 🔗

Add the path to mofography to your python path in your scripts and notebooks before you import,


import sys
import os
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath('path_to_mofography'))

of course, replace path_to_mofography with the relative path to the mofography directory on your local machine. This way we are not installing anything yet, so if there are changes to the source code, you can simply pull the latest changes using git pull and use them withouth having to reinstall the package everytime. ### Test the installation 🧪 - Import mofography to see if it works. There are CIF files in themofography/examples/TestCIFs` folder, which you can use to test the package. Let’s use a full-on clustering workflow with default parameters on the IRMOF-1 structure. More information on the inner workings of the workflow are provided in the Quick cluster tutorial.

import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
mat_atoms = read('path_to_mofography/examples/TestCIFs/P1-IRMOF-1.cif')
figures = mgr.quick_cluster(mat_atoms)

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text: In thie notebook, we’ll load up a dataset of MOFs, such as the IZA database, create ASE atoms objects from it, create a workflow for a single materials and finally extend and parallelize it over the whole dataset using Dask. This notebook uses a ‘local’ cluster, meaning your personal laptop or desktop with a single CPU, however, the same code can be used to scale up to a cluster with many CPUs or GPUs. Please refer the Dask documentation for more information on how to set up a cluster here: https://docs.dask.org

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
Imports and Paths
Let’s import the necessary libraries and set some paths

#* General imports
import os, sys

text:
Load the dataset
I have the dataset saved up, if you don’t have it, check out hte getting data from MOFDB tutuorial to create and save the dataframe.

iza_df = pd.read_feather('C:/Users/Arun Gopalan/OneDrive - The University of Manchester/my_cloned_repos/mofography/examples/iza_df.feather')

the dataset looks like this:

print(iza_df.columns)
iza_df.head(10)


## Create ASE atoms objects from the dataframe


iza_atoms = mgr.atoms_from_mofdb_df(iza_df)


## Create a workflow for a single material
# Let's pick one random material and define our usual workflow where we create pore graphs from the atoms object. If this looks unfamiliar, please refer to the previous tutorials.


mat_atoms = iza_atoms[3] # you can try other materials also


# compute bonds
mat_updated  = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(mat_atoms)
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(mat_atoms, spacing=0.5) #* compute distance grid
shape = dgrid.shape #* we'll need this for later
regions, maxima = mgr.regions_from_dgrid(dgrid, mask_thickness=1.0) #* compute regions
maxima_radii = dgrid[tuple(maxima.T)] #* grab the radii of the maxima from dgrid
regions_pbc  = mgr.apply_pbc(regions, maxima, maxima_radii, mat_atoms, return_conn=False) #* apply PBC and return as 3D array
pbc_groups = mgr.apply_pbc(regions, maxima, maxima_radii, mat_atoms, return_conn=True) #* return as connected groups
rag = mgr.get_rag_from_regions_and_grid(regions, dgrid, mat_atoms, maxima) #* create pore graph
rag = mgr.add_maxima_to_rag(rag, maxima, maxima_radii, shape, mat_atoms) #* add maxima to the graph
rag = mgr.add_pbc_to_rag(rag, pbc_groups) #* add PBC information to the graph
connections = mgr.get_connections_for_rag(rag, regions, maxima, mat_atoms, dgrid) #* compute windows


rag.graph['mat_atoms'] = mat_atoms
rag.graph['dgrid'] = dgrid
rag.graph['regions'] = regions
rag.graph['maxima'] = maxima
rag.graph['maxima_radii'] = maxima_radii
rag.graph['regions_pbc'] = regions_pbc
rag.graph['pbc_groups'] = pbc_groups
rag.graph['connections'] = connections


frame_trace = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated, stylize=True)
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_updated)
maxima_trace = mgr.plot_maxima(dgrid, maxima, mat_atoms)
surface_regions = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid, isovalue=1.5, ase_atoms = mat_atoms, region_labels=regions, stylize=True)
rag_trace = mgr.plot_rag(rag)

fig = go.Figure(data=[*frame_trace, cell_trace, maxima_trace, surface_regions, rag_trace], layout=mgr.epic_layout)
fig.update_scenes(aspectmode='data')
fig.show()

text:
Start a dask cluster locally.
Look at the dask documentation for more information on how to set up a cluster on a remote machine or a cloud service or to change the number of workers, processes, threads etc.

cluster = LocalCluster()
client = Client(cluster)

print('THe client is running on : ', client.dashboard_link)

IF you go to the link, you’ll see something like this: https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/dashboard.html. You can see the progress of the workflow and the resources being used.

#* submit the workflow using the futures API

futures = dask.persist(*delayed_rag_futures) 


#* quick progress tracking, run this cell again for updates after any errors

progress(futures)

after the workflow is done, we can grab the results like this

results = client.compute(futures)

grab the results for finished futures. If some are still running or errored, let’s set them to None

rags = [r.result() if r.status == 'finished' else None for r in results]

Check how many of them failed
(np.array(rags) == None).sum()
Notice that some of them failed, this is OK, it is just to show how to handle errors (the updated routines don’t fail as much :)). Let’s just redefine the workflow with updated functions where will compute the edges and windows first and then make a graph from that, instead of using RAG functions from skimage.

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
section: Redefine the workflow with different functions
text:
Redefine the workflow with different functions

connections = mgr.connections_from_regions_and_dgrid(regions, dgrid, maxima, mat_atoms)
rag  = mgr.rag_from_connections(connections, maxima)

#* rest of the steps are the same

Now, let’s redefine the workflow using dask delayed like before, notice the change in the order of the calculations before: dgrid -> regions -> maxima -> regions_pbc -> rag -> connections -> rest of the steps after: dgrid -> regions -> maxima -> connections -> rag-> rest of the steps

def make_rag_updated(regions, dgrid, maxima,maxima_radii, mat_atoms):
    connections = mgr.connections_from_regions_and_dgrid(regions, dgrid, maxima, mat_atoms)
    rag = mgr.rag_from_connections(connections, maxima)
    shape = dgrid.shape
    rag = mgr.add_maxima_to_rag(rag, maxima, maxima_radii, shape, mat_atoms)
    rag.graph['dgrid'] = dgrid
    rag.graph['regions'] = regions
    rag.graph['maxima'] = maxima
    rag.graph['ase_atoms'] = mat_atoms
    rag.graph['connections'] = connections

    return rag

delayed_rag_futures = [] 

for mat_atoms in iza_atoms:
    dgrid = delayed(mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu)(mat_atoms, spacing=0.5, precompute=True)
    # dgrid = delayed(mgr.zoom_grid)(dgrid, 2.0) #* let's zoom the grid make it finer using interpolation
    regions_maxima_radii = delayed(regions_maxima_radii_from_dgrid)(dgrid, mask_thickness=0.5)
    regions_pbc = delayed(mgr.apply_pbc)(regions_maxima_radii[0], regions_maxima_radii[1], regions_maxima_radii[2], mat_atoms)
    #* notice the change in the wrapping function here, defined above
    rag = delayed(make_rag_updated)(regions_maxima_radii[0], dgrid, regions_maxima_radii[1], regions_maxima_radii[2], mat_atoms)
    delayed_rag_futures.append(rag)


delayed_rag_futures[0].compute()


client = Client(LocalCluster())

print('THe client is running on : ', client.dashboard_link)


futures= dask.persist(*delayed_rag_futures)


results = client.compute(futures)
rags = [r.result() if r.status == 'finished' else None for r in results]


def connections_from_regions_and_dgrid(region_labels, dgrid, maxima, ase_atoms, wall_windows=True, distance_threshold=1.0, wall_thickness=2):

    """
    It takes a 3D array of region labels, a list of maxima, an ASE atoms object, and a distance
    threshold, and returns a list of connections between regions, and the centers of the windows between
    them
    
    :param region_labels: The labels of the regions, as returned by the skimage.measure.label function
    :param maxima: the maxima of the image
    :param ase_atoms: ASE atoms object
    :param wall_windows: If True, then the windows on the wall are also calculated, defaults to True
    (optional)
    :param distance_threshold: The distance threshold for the agglomerative clustering
    :return: A list of connections between regions.
    """

    def check_connected(regs):
            
        import numpy as np
        from icecream import ic
        ic.disable()
        from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering

        j = regs[1]

        if np.sum(check_flag) > 0:
            # print("Edges found between "+str(i)+' and '+ str(j) + ' sum: '+str(np.sum(check_flag)))
            windices = np.vstack(np.where(check_flag)).T  # * (N,3)
            window_points = np.dot(A_unit, (windices / region_labels.shape).T).T  # * (N,3)
            # ic(window_points)
            # * No clustering
            # window_centers = np.mean(window_points, axis=0)
            
            # * DBScan
            # X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(window_points)
            # db = DBSCAN(eps=0.5, min_samples=10).fit(X_scaled)
            # window_centers = np.vstack([window_points[db.labels_==i].mean(axis=0) for i in np.unique(db.labels_) if i != -1])
            
            # if len(window_points) >1:
            # * Agglomerative
            ag = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=None, linkage='single',distance_threshold=minimum_window_separation, compute_full_tree=True).fit(window_points)
            #* we are taking the centroid of the clusters here as the window location
            # window_centers = np.vstack([window_points[ag.labels_==i].mean(axis=0) for i in np.unique(ag.labels_) if i != -1])
            
            # * what if we took the index of the point where the distance value is the largest in the window boundary region, that way we don't have to worry bout
            #* regions at the wall
            d_windices = dgrid[tuple(windices.T)] # distance values at the window indices
            r_windices =region_labels[tuple(windices.T)] # region labels at the window indices
            # window_centers = [(window_points[np.argmax(d_windices[np.logical_and(r_windices[ag.labels_ == uwi]==regs[0],ag.labels_==uwi)])] + window_points[np.argmax(d_windices[np.logical_and(r_windices[ag.labels_==uwi]==regs[1],ag.labels_==uwi)])])/2.0 for uwi in np.unique(ag.labels_) if uwi != -1]

            # print('These are window centers', window_centers)
            window_centers = []
            for uwi in np.unique(ag.labels_):
                # for each cluster that is nota noise, do this 
                if uwi != -1:
                    # np.argmax(d_windices[ag.labels_==uwi])



                    uwi_dvals = d_windices[ag.labels_==uwi] # distance values in the cluster with label uwi
                    uwi_points = window_points[ag.labels_==uwi] # points in the cluster with label uwi
                    uwi_r = r_windices[ag.labels_==uwi]
                    
                    # for points in first region

                    # uwi_r1_indices =np.transpose((uwi_r==regs[0])).nonzero()
                    uwi_r1_indices =(np.where)(uwi_r==regs[0])[0]
                    # print('uwi_r1_indices are ', uwi_r1_indices)
                    # print(uwi_r1_indices.shape)
                    uwi_r1_dvals = uwi_dvals[uwi_r1_indices]
                    uwi_r1_points = uwi_points[uwi_r1_indices]
                    uwi_r1_max_indices = np.argmax(uwi_r1_dvals) #np.where(uwi_r1_dvals == np.max(uwi_r1_dvals))[0] # indices of the maximum distance values in the cluster with label uwi
                    # print(uwi_r1_max_indices)
                    uwi_r1_max_points = uwi_r1_points[uwi_r1_max_indices]

                    
                    
                    # for points in second region
                    uwi_r2_indices =(np.where)(uwi_r==regs[1])[0]
                    uwi_r2_dvals = uwi_dvals[uwi_r2_indices]
                    uwi_r2_points = uwi_points[uwi_r2_indices]
                    uwi_r2_max_indices = np.where(uwi_r2_dvals == np.max(uwi_r2_dvals))[0] # indices of the maximum distance values in the cluster with label uwi
                    uwi_r2_max_points = uwi_r2_points[uwi_r2_max_indices]

                    uwi_center = (uwi_r1_max_points + uwi_r2_max_points)/2

                    # uwi_center = np.mean(uwi_max_points, axis=0) # mean of the points where the distance is at maximum if ther are multiple a.k.a the window is symmetric on each side

                    window_centers.append(uwi_center) 

            # window_centers = np.vstack(window_centers)
        # else:
            # window_centers = window_points
            window_centers = np.vstack(window_centers)
            window_fractional = get_fractional_coordinates(window_centers,ase_atoms)
            window_fractional = np.round(window_fractional, decimals=4)

            return np.array([regs, True,'internal', window_centers, window_radii], dtype='object') # returns a list of [[r1,r2], connected or not, array of window_centers]

    import numpy as np

    import ase
    # from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

    A_unit = ase.geometry.complete_cell(ase_atoms.get_cell()).T
    from icecream import ic
    minimum_window_separation = distance_threshold
        
    dinterp = interpolate_dgrid(dgrid)
    # * Find the outer boundary of each individual region
    regions_to_check = np.delete(np.unique(region_labels),0)
    ic(regions_to_check)
    # outer = {reg:find_boundaries(region_labels == reg, mode='outer') for reg in regions_to_check}
    outer = {reg:find_boundaries(region_labels == reg, mode='outer') for reg in regions_to_check}
    ic(len(outer))
    # * Check for connectedness between regions
    check_list = np.vstack(list(itertools.combinations(regions_to_check, 2))) # list of pairs of region labels
    connections_list = [check_connected(c) for c in check_list] # now this step could cause an overflow
    # connections_list = db.from_sequence(check_list).map(check_connected).compute()
    
    # connected_regions = [[c[0], [c[2]] for c in connections_list if c[1] == True] # Make a new list with all the 
    
    #* Windows on the wall are to be calculated
    if wall_windows:
        wwl= get_wall_windows2(regions=region_labels, maxima=maxima, dgrid=dgrid, ase_atoms=ase_atoms, wall_thickness=wall_thickness)
        if len(wwl)>0:
            connections_list.append(wwl)


    # #* we have one final thing to do 
    # # * if both the regions forming an internal window are on the same wall, then we need to set the window center and the radius to 
    # # * that on the wall, since centroid


    # for c in connections_list:
    #     if np.logical_and(c[1], c[2]=='internal'):

    return np.vstack(connections_list)


def interpolate_dgrid(dgrid):
    """Create a scipy.interpolator.RegularGridInterpolator, using 'nearest' method for the region labels (or any 3D numpy grid) 
    over a unit box ([0,1]) in all axes.

    :param regions: 3D numpy array of region labels
    :type regions: numpy.array 
    :return: a scipy RegularGridInterpolator object that works on the fractional coordinates of atoms
    :rtype: scipy.interpolate.RegularGridInterpolator
    """    
    import numpy as np
    from scipy.interpolate import RegularGridInterpolator as RGI
    xx = np.linspace(0,  1,dgrid.shape[0])
    yy = np.linspace(0,  1,dgrid.shape[1])
    zz = np.linspace(0,  1,dgrid.shape[2])
    dl = RGI((xx, yy, zz),dgrid, method='linear')

    return dl

def get_wall_windows2(regions, maxima, dgrid, ase_atoms, wall_thickness=2):
    import numpy as np
    from icecream import ic
    # from .helper import find_coord_from_indices, interpolate_labels
    wall_windows = []
    shape =regions.shape
    dinterp =interpolate_dgrid(dgrid)
    for a in [0,1,2]:
        ic.disable()
        ic(a)
        llr = regions.take(indices=0 ,axis=a) #* left wall
        llr_d = dgrid.take(indices=0, axis=a) #* left wall distances 
        rrr = regions.take(indices=shape[a]-1 ,axis=a)  #* right wall
        rrr_d = dgrid.take(indices=shape[a]-1, axis=a) #* right wall distances 

        map_list = np.unique(list(zip(llr.flatten(), rrr.flatten())), axis=0)
        not_background = [m for m in map_list if np.all(m!=0)]
        # * there should be some non background mappings in the direction
        if len(not_background) > 0:
            map_list = np.vstack([m for m in map_list if np.all(m!=0)])

            # * flags to check whether it is window or a just a pocket split across walls
            flags = np.vstack([[maxima[k - 1][a]>wall_thickness, maxima[v-1][a]<(shape[a]-wall_thickness)] for k,v in map_list])    
            
            # * this line makes sure maxima are both well inside
            flags = np.logical_and(flags[:,0],flags[:,1])
            
            # window_indices = [np.vstack(np.where(llr==m[0])).mean(axis=1) for i,m in enumerate(map_list) if flags[i]]
            wregs_l  = [(np.array([m[0], m[1]]), True,'periodic') for i, m in enumerate(map_list) if flags[i]]
            wregs_r  = [(np.array([m[1], m[0]]), True,'periodic') for i, m in enumerate(map_list) if flags[i]]
            # instead of taking the mean of the points at the left wall, let's find the location of the maximum in the distance
            # values for the points on that plan
            # window_indices = [np.vstack(np.where(llr==m[0])).mean(axis=1).T for i, m in enumerate(map_list) if flags[i]]
            window_indices_list = [np.argwhere(llr==m[0]) for i, m in enumerate(map_list) if flags[i]]
            window_indices = [indices[np.argmax(llr_d[indices[:,0], indices[:,1]])] for indices in window_indices_list]

            # print('Detected wall windows are :{}'.format(window_indices))

            ic(window_indices)
            if np.any(flags):
                window_indices_l = np.insert(np.vstack(window_indices), [a], np.zeros((len(window_indices),1)), axis=1  )
                window_indices_r = np.insert(np.vstack(window_indices), [a], (shape[a] -1)*np.ones((len(window_indices),1)), axis=1 )
                window_radii_l = np.vstack(dinterp(window_indices_l/regions.shape))
                window_radii_r = np.vstack(dinterp(window_indices_r/regions.shape))
                window_coords_l = find_coord_from_indices(window_indices_l, shape=shape, ase_atoms=ase_atoms)
                window_coords_r = find_coord_from_indices(window_indices_r, shape=shape, ase_atoms=ase_atoms)
                ic(window_coords_l)
                ic(window_coords_r)
                window_rows_l = np.vstack([[*w, np.array([ window_coords_l[i] ]), window_radii_l[i]] for i,w in enumerate(wregs_l)])
                window_rows_r = np.vstack([[*w, np.array([ window_coords_r[i] ]), window_radii_r[i]] for i,w in enumerate(wregs_r)])
                wall_windows.append(window_rows_l) 
                wall_windows.append(window_rows_r) 
                
    if len(wall_windows)>0:
        wall_windows =  np.vstack(wall_windows)
    

    return wall_windows
def rag_from_connections(connections, maxima, only_use_internal=True):
    
    """ Create a basic networkx graph (with no properties annotated) from the array of connections
    :type connections: np.array of shape (Nregions-Choose-2 ,1) where Nregions is the number of unique regions. Each row has 
    three elements, the region indices [r1, r2], a boolean flag showing whether they are connected, and window coordinate(s) if the regions are connected, and None is they are not.
    :param connections: numpy array

    :raises:

    :rtype: a graph object of the class networkx.Graph
    """
    import networkx as nx 
    import numpy as np
    G = nx.Graph()
    # number_of_regions = np.max([c[0] for c  in connections])
    number_of_nodes = len(maxima) #np.max([c[0] for c  in connections])
    # print(number_of_nodes)
    # nx.set_node_attributes(G, values={i+1:i+1 for i in range(number_of_nodes)}, name='labels')
    G.add_nodes_from(range(1, number_of_nodes+1)) 
    if only_use_internal:# range stops one short
        G.add_edges_from([c[0] for c in connections if np.logical_and(c[1], c[2] =='internal')])
    else:
        G.add_edges_from([c[0] for c in connections if c[1]])
    # add labels property to rag
    nx.set_node_attributes(G, values={i+1:[i+1] for i in range(len(G.nodes))}, name='labels')
    return G


connections = mgr.connections_from_regions_and_dgrid(regions, dgrid, maxima, mat_atoms)


connections

title: Computing the Distance Grid
text:
In this tutorial, one of the most useful and foundational calculations in mofography, the distance grid. The distance grid refers to a 3D array of floating point values, where the value in each voxel corresponds to the shortest distance to the nearest framework surface. Of course, the definition of framework surface requires assigning some radii to the atoms of the material. By default, mofography uses the covalent radii of the atoms, but you can also use the van der Waals radii or some other mixed and matched set of radii, as we will see shortly. So, in this tutorial we will see the following:
The first few steps are same as before, so we won’t be explaining them in detail here, please refer to the Basic structure IO tutorial for more details.

title: Computing the Distance Grid
text:
Computing the distance grid
The most important parameter in computing the grid is the grid spacing. This is the fineness of your grid, and is input as the distance between adjacent voxels in angstroms. The finer the grid, the more accurate the calculations, although, keep in mind that, - when you reduce the grid spacing by a factor of 2, the number of voxels in the grid increases by a factor of 8. - all the subsequent calculations would also be more expensive, since the grid is larger.

Calculation under the hood

On a CPU: mofography uses Dask to paralellize the grid calcuation for efficiency. Hence, the returned object is a Dask array, which can be converted to a numpy array using the compute() method. On top of that, mofography borrows the AABB cell list algorithm from Freud, to further speed up the calculation manifold.

Some information about the function

help(mgr.dgrid_from_atoms)

Help on function dgrid_from_atoms in module mofography.compute:

dgrid_from_atoms(ase_atoms, radii=None, spacing=0.25, block_size=50000, n_neighbors=10, probe_radius=0)
    Compute distance grid from ase atoms objects
    
    :param ase_atoms: ASE atoms object
    :type ase_atoms: ase.atoms
    :param spacing: fineness of the grid in angstrom, defaults to 0.25
    :type spacing: float, optional
    :param chunksize: number of grid points per block of the dask grid. Usually a tradeoff between fewer blocks 
    and data transfer limitation from large blocksizes, defaults to 50000
    :type chunksize: int, optional
    :param n_neighbors: number of neighbors to check for distance, fewer the faster, but risk getting wrong distance 
    since the neighbor sorting by default uses the center to center distance and does not account for the atomic radii, defaults to 10
    :type n_neighbors: int, optional
    :param probe_radius: size of the probe for computing distace to framework surface, defaults to 0.0 corresponding to a point probe
    :type probe_radius: float, optional
    :return: Grid of shape (nx, ny, nz), wher nx, ny, nz are the number of grid points corresponding to the spacing specified earlier
    :rtype: 3D numpy array

Tips and tricks #1
In parallel computing, it is pivotal to divide the calculation into pieces of the right size. If the pieces are too small, the overhead of the parallelization is too high, and if the pieces are too large, the parallelization is not effective. The chunk_size parameter in the compute() method allows you to specify the size of the chunks. The default value is 50000 which is a good starting point. If you are running into memory issues, you can reduce this value. If your RAM is not being fully utilized, you can increase this value, if your RAM is too small, you may want to reduce this value.


Tips and tricks #2
By default, mofography uses a point probe, meaning it has no size. If you’d like a different probe, like argon, you can specify it using the probe_radius parameter. We will leave that as an exercise.


Tips and tricks #3
If you have a lot of atoms in your unit cell, you may want to reduce the n_neighbors parameter, it will make the calculation of the AABB cell list faster. The default value is 10, which is a good starting point. Since we want the probe-to-framework, surface-to-surface distance, and not the center-to-center distance, we should consider a few center-to-center neighbors while checking for the one with the shortest surface-to-surface distance.

On a GPU (+CPU): If you have a powerful nvidia GPU, we might be able to take advantage of that to speed up the calculation. The GPU routine is quite similar to the CPU routine, but doesn’t use the cell list algorithm, for memory management reasons. Essentially, it breaks down the calculation onto different cores of the CPU, and then each core talks to the GPU independently to do the calculation. It uses a CuPy backend to do the calculations on the GPU. Unlike the CPU version, it returns a CuPy array. You can convert it to a numpy array using the asnumpy() function. Still, you might get a speed up over the CPU routine. Let’s look at it in action

title: Computing the Distance Grid
text:
Visualizing the distance grid
Usually plotting a 3D volume is computationally expensive and often unclear. Instead, we can plot and isosurface of the distance grid, which is a surface that is at a certain constant distance from the framework surface. This is a much more intuitive way to visualize the distance grid. Let’s look at how to do that in mofography.

A note on the renderer
In Plotly you can have many different renderers, in this tutorial we are using renderer='png' to save some space by rendering as a static image. Instead to get an interactive plot, you can use renderer='notebook_connected' or renderer='browser' to get an interactive plot in the notebook or in a separate browser tab respectively.

help(mgr.plot_surface_dgrid)

Help on function plot_surface_dgrid in module mofography.visualize:

plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid, isovalue, ase_atoms, region_labels=None, select='all', opacity=1.0, cscale=None, color='blue', stepsize=1, stylize=False, random_seed=0, hover_label='Region :', **kwargs_mesh)
    It takes a 3D grid, an isovalue, an ASE atoms object, and a few other optional parameters and
    returns a plotly mesh3d object that can be plotted using plotly
    
    Args:
      dgrid: the density grid
      isovalue: the value of the isosurface to be plotted
      ase_atoms: ASE atoms object
      region_labels: a 3D array of the same shape as the density grid. Each voxel in the density grid is
    assigned a label. The labels are used to color the surface.
      select: a list of region labels to plot. If 'all' is selected, all regions are plotted. Defaults
    to all
      opacity: The opacity of the surface.
      cscale: a colorscale for the regions. If None, a random colorscale is generated.
      color: color of the cell. Defaults to blue
      stepsize: The step size for the marching cubes algorithm. Defaults to 1
      stylize: if True, will apply some random style choices, purely personal preference. Defaults to
    False
      random_seed: This is used to generate the random colors for the regions. If you want to reproduce
    the same colors, use the same random seed. Defaults to 0
    
    Returns:
      a plotly mesh3d object.

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Note: These tutorials are not a substitute for reading the paper. For details on the algorithms working under the hood, please read the original publication. However, these tutorials are useful for learning the syntax of mofography
In this tutorial, we will learn how to find the connections between the different cavities in a material, locate the one or more adjoining pore windows, and to finally visualize them along with everything else that we have seen so far.
Finding the pore windows is an involved calculation, hence we need everything we have computed so far to get the pore windows, we need - The distance grid - the local maxima of the distance grid - the region segmentation grid - the distance values at the local maxima - the pore graph
To give some brief insights into the window finding algorithm in mofography, we locate the windows as the centroid of the points in the shared outer boundary of two touching regions. There are couple of nuances to window finding,
As before, we won’t be explaining the steps that we have already covered in the previous tutorials, if anything is unclear, please refer to the previous tutorials.

title: Applying Periodic Boundary Conditions
text:
In this notebook, we will see how to apply periodic boundary conditions to the 3D grid of region segmentation from the earlier tutorial. So if you haven’t tried the ‘Region segmentation’ tutorial, please do so before proceeding with this one. In this tutorial, we will simply rush through the steps with no explanation up until the point where we have the 3D grid of region segmentation.
Periodic Boundary Conditions (PBC) is useful for improving our intuitive understanding of the cavities in a material, averaging the pore properties correctly, and makes it possible to work with one unit cell of the material instead of having to replicate the unit cell multiple times (for materials where the structure can be treated as rigid).
Applying PBC, is probably the most error prone step in the cavity type detection workflow, since materials can have a variety of pore structures and the application of PBC can be tricky as we will see shortly.

title: Applying Periodic Boundary Conditions
section: The meaning of PBC in this context
text:
The meaning of PBC in this context
To understand a bit more clearly what I mean by applying PBC, let’s visualize the current segmentation using a 1.75 \(\AA\) isosurface like before

import plotly.graph_objects as go 
import plotly.express as px 

cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel

isosurface_trace= mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid.compute(), ase_atoms=mat_updated,isovalue=1.75, cscale=cscale, opacity=1, stylize=True, region_labels=regions)
cell_trace  = mgr.plot_cell(mat_updated)

fig = go.Figure(data=[isosurface_trace, cell_trace])

fig.update_layout(mgr.dark_layout)
fig.show(renderer='png')








As you can see there are 8 pockets in this unit cell - One at the center - 1/8 at each corner, and 8 corners to the unit cell: 1/8 * 8 = 1 - 1/4 at each edge, and 12 edges to the unit cell: 1/4 * 12 = 3 - 1/2 at each face, and 6 faces to the unit cell: 1/2 * 6 = 3
Intuitively, we know this. And in order to average the properties correctly, our algorithm needs to recognize such information. mofography has a collection of novel algorithms implemented in it to check whether pairs of regions are connected by periodic boundary conditions or not. To summarize, PBC asks the following question:
Which segmented pockets at the wall come together to form a complete cavity as per periodic boundary conditions?
Let’s simply run the PBC algorithm on the segmentation and see what happens. Note that the output is another 3D grid of the same size as the input, where each voxel is assigned a label corresponding to the periodic group it belongs to. Each group is a set of regions that are connected by PBC. One additionaly thing we need to do this estimation in mofography is the size of the local maxima, which we already have from the distance grid.

maxima_radii  = dgrid.compute()[tuple(maxima.T)]
regions_pbc = mgr.apply_pbc(regions, maxima, maxima_radii, mat_atoms)

Now, let’s visualize the results again using a 1.75 \(\AA\) isosurface

import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px

cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel

isosurface_trace = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid.compute(), ase_atoms=mat_updated,
                                          isovalue=1.75, cscale=cscale, opacity=1, stylize=True, region_labels=regions_pbc)
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_updated)

fig = go.Figure(data=[isosurface_trace, cell_trace])

fig.update_layout(mgr.dark_layout)
fig.show(renderer='png')








Now everything in the same pbc groups is colored the same. We can also look at the PBC groups, like this

pbc_groups = mgr.apply_pbc(regions, maxima, maxima_radii, mat_atoms, return_conn=True)
pbc_groups

[{1, 3, 7, 9, 19, 21, 25, 27},
 {2, 8, 20, 26},
 {4, 5, 22, 24},
 {6, 23},
 {10, 11, 13, 15},
 {12, 17},
 {14, 16},
 {18}]


We can see that there are 8 groups, and each group has 1-8 pockets, depending on whether it is at the corner, edge, face or center. This is exactly what we expect.

title: Applying Periodic Boundary Conditions
text:
Tunable parameters
There are basically two tunable parameters in the PBC algorithm, the wall_thickness and the minimum_overlap_fraction. The wall_thickness is the thickness of the wall in angstroms that will be considered when looking to for regions to connect via PBC. The minimum_overlap_fraction is the minimum fraction of wall projection of one region that needs to overlap with the wall projection of another region on the opposite wall for them to be considered connected by PBC. Note that this is checked in both directions, so if the overlap fraction is 0.5, then the regions need to overlap by at least 0.5 in at least one of the directions.
Feel free to experiment with these parameters, but the default values should work well for most cases.

title: Applying Periodic Boundary Conditions
text:
A bit more complex example
The IRMOF-1 structure was great in recognizing the PBC connected pockets, but the pore structure in materials can be way more complex. Let’s put mofography to test to one of the more complex cases of NU-1000


path_to_cif = os.path.join(path_to_mgr, 'examples','TestCIFs', 'NU-1000_S1.cif')

mat_atoms = read(path_to_cif)

dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms(mat_updated, spacing=0.25)

Covalent Bonds
mofography provdes a shorthand subroutine for detecing the covalent bonds in the structure, which quite useful for analysis and visualization. By default, it looks for atomic distances that are lesser than the sum of the covalent radii of the two atoms and considers that a bond. The following example shows how to detect the bonds in a structure using mofography



mat_updated = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(mat_atoms)

title: Basic Structure Operations : IO, Structure graph and Pattern matching
text:
Structure graph
Structure graph is networkx graph object, formed using atoms as nodes and bonds as edges. Mofography offers a simple routine to generate a strcture graph from an ASE atoms object. - Having a structure graph is quite useful for analysing the structure at hand, such as detecting chemical moeties such functional groups, rings (aromatic and otherwise). - Annotating the atoms and bonds with relevant information, to be used in conjuction with other routines or tools. Sgraph is a simpler version of the pymatgen structure graph, put in place to perform complex structure manipulations in the future.

mat_sgraph = mgr.sgraph_from_atoms(mat_updated)

matching = mgr.find_pattern_in_sgraph(mat_sgraph, nx.subgraph(mat_sgraph,small_cycles[0]))

title: Detect functional groups in MOFs
text:
In this notebook, we will use mofography to detect sepecifc functional groups in MOFs. We will then extend this to look for functional groups in a database of MOFs such as the CoRE MOF database. ### Algorithm
Under the hood, mofography uses a graph-based approach to detect functional groups. The algorithm is called subgraph isomorphism and is a well-known problem in computer science. The algorithm is implemented in the networkx package. Detection occurs based on element and bond types. The source code is in analyze.py in the mofography package.

Apply to CoRE MOFs in High Throughput
Now let’s try to apply the functional group detection to the whole list of coremof atoms objects we compiled in the beginning of the notebook. We will look for a few common single-ring aromatic groups in the materials in the list. And to speed things up, and to make sure that our workflow won’t fail even if one or more of the calculations fail, we’ll use the ‘futures’ API from Dask. You can expect another detailed tutorial on using Dask for high throughput materials workflows coming soon.
For me, It took about 30 minutes for about 7500 coremof materials on a core i7 laptop. Your mileage will vary depending on your hardware and the number of materials you’re screening.
(PS: Notice that, if you have multiple functional groups, you can screen for them all at the same time, not one by one.😂)

title: Graph Convolution on RAGs to predict adsorption isotherms
text:
NOte: Only works with Numpy 1.23.* for now, will fix soon.
In this notebook, we will start from scratch, create a dataset of pore graphs, learn a graph embedding for these pore graphs using Graph Convolutional Net, trained such that the embedding will accurately predict (or try to) hydrogen adsorption of the IZA dataset based on the data pre tabulated in MOFDB. Once we have a working model, we will estimate it’s accuracy, and also do hyper parameter tuning using Bayesian Optimization as implemented in Optuna. Then we can try to grab a bunch of CoRE MOFs and try to see how well the model can predict the hydrogen isotherms. In theory, the embedding learned this way is pretty much a latent space for you to use as an input for other more complex adsorption applications.
This tutorial is really really long, since we are building the dataset from scratch. Once you have the dataset, next time you run it, you can load up the pickle file and resume the workflow from there, that should be much faster.
Here are the approximate steps in this monstrosity 1. Make imports and set paths 2. Load the IZA dataset from MOFDB 3. Create RAGs, - compute dgrid - compute regions and maxima - compute pbc - compute connections - compte rag - add maxima and pbc to rag - add energy interpolator to rag 4. Do clustering of pockets on the pore graphs using energy values using precalculated interpolators 5. Add energy histograms to pore graphs keeping the bins the same across materials (of course, we need this to do machine learning) 6. Define Graph convolutional network that outputs the embeddings using Deep Graph Library 7. Train the model to predict adsorption at the highest pressure point 8. Estimate and plot the parity 10. Train the model to predict adsorption at all 8 pressures 11. Estimate and plot the average error and std deviation at each pressure point 12. Hyperparameter tuning We wil tune the learning rate, number of hidden units, droput ratio, weigh decay ratio, and the choice of activation function using Optuna as a black box 13. Predict isotherms for a new set of pore graphs like coremofs for example, compiling this dataset is left as an excercise to the reader. the code for predicting is here.
Unlike usual tutorials, I am not quite going into the details of each step, you can ask chat gpt is something is unclear.
PS: The reason for splitting up the dataset creation workflow is to avoid memory bottlenecks while passing around large energy interpolators or accidentally running the energ calculation over a single core instead of in parallel due to poor distribution. Just follow along and you shall be fine (mostly).

MOre wrapper functions for Dask, and to store the calculated things into the pore graph. Note that the storing function is called only at the end of the workflow for each material.

def regions_maxima_radii_from_dgrid(dgrid, mask_thickness = 1.0):
    regions, maxima = mgr.regions_from_dgrid(dgrid, mask_thickness = mask_thickness)
    maxima_radii = dgrid[tuple(maxima.T )]
    return regions, maxima, maxima_radii


def make_rag_upto_pbc(regions, dgrid, maxima,maxima_radii, mat_atoms, pbc_groups):
    connections = mgr.connections_from_regions_and_dgrid(regions, dgrid, maxima, mat_atoms)
    rag = mgr.rag_from_connections(connections, maxima, only_use_internal=False)
    shape = dgrid.shape
    rag = mgr.add_maxima_to_rag(rag, maxima, maxima_radii, shape, mat_atoms)
    rag = mgr.add_pbc_to_rag(rag, pbc_groups)
    props = regionprops(regions)
    rag = mgr.add_centroids_to_rag_with_pbc(rag,props, pbc_groups, mat_atoms, regions.shape)
    # einterp = make_einterp(mat_atoms)
    # rag = mgr.add_vdw_hist_to_rag(rag, regions, energy_interpolator=einterp, use_pbc=True, pbc_groups = pbc_groups)
    rag = mgr.add_pbc_to_rag(rag, pbc_groups)
    rag.graph['dgrid'] = dgrid
    rag.graph['regions'] = regions
    rag.graph['maxima'] = maxima
    rag.graph['ase_atoms'] = mat_atoms
    rag.graph['connections'] = connections
    rag.graph['pbc_groups'] = pbc_groups
    rag.graph['einterp'] = einterp
    return rag
def make_einterp(mat_atoms):
    egrid = mgr.egrid_from_atoms2(mat_atoms, spacing=0.5, probe_symbol='He', precompute=False)
    # einterp = mgr.interpolate_dgrid(egrid)
    einterp = mgr.get_energy_interpolator(egrid)
    return einterp

text:
Hyperparameter optimization
Let’s do some hyper parameter tuning using Optuna, since, graph netwroks are notorious for over fitting and given our small dataset, we probably overfit the heck out of it. I am doing only 50 trials, you can do more

class GCN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_feats, hidden_size, num_classes, dropout, activation):
        super(GCN, self).__init__()
        self.conv1 = GraphConv(in_feats, hidden_size, activation=activation)
        self.conv2 = GraphConv(hidden_size, num_classes)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout)

    def forward(self, g, features):
        x = self.conv1(g, features)
        x = self.dropout(x)
        x = self.conv2(g, x)
        return x
import optuna

def objective(trial):
    # Suggest values for the hyperparameters
    hidden_size = trial.suggest_int('hidden_size', 16, 128)
    lr = trial.suggest_loguniform('lr', 1e-5, 1e-1)
    dropout = trial.suggest_uniform('dropout', 0.0, 1.0)
    weight_decay = trial.suggest_loguniform('weight_decay', 1e-9, 1e-3)
    activation_name = trial.suggest_categorical('activation', ['relu', 'tanh', 'sigmoid'])
    activation = getattr(F, activation_name)

    # Initialize the model and optimizer
    model = GCN(features.size(1), hidden_size, 8, dropout, activation)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)

    # Training loop
    for epoch in range(1000):
        model.train()
        embeddings = model(batched_graph, features)
        batched_graph.ndata['h'] = embeddings
        logits = dgl.mean_nodes(batched_graph, 'h')
        loss = F.mse_loss(logits, labels, reduction='mean')
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        # Handle pruning based on the intermediate value.
        if trial.should_prune():
            raise optuna.exceptions.TrialPruned()

    return loss.item()

study = optuna.create_study(direction='minimize', pruner=optuna.pruners.HyperbandPruner())
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50)

print('Best trial:')
trial = study.best_trial
print('  Value: ', trial.value)
print('  Params: ')
for key, value in trial.params.items():
    print('    {}: {}'.format(key, value))

Predict for new graphs
I’ll leave this as an exercise, just do the same steps to compile a list of new pore graphs from CIF files, put it as new_graphs are and predict their isotherms like shown below:

# Assume we have some new NetworkX graphs in a list `new_graphs`
new_graphs = [...]

# Convert NetworkX graphs to DGL graphs and set node features
new_dgl_graphs = []
for g in new_graphs:
    if g is not None:
        dgl_g = dgl.from_networkx(g)
        dgl_g = dgl.add_self_loop(dgl_g)  # Add self-loops
        dgl_g.ndata['feat'] = torch.tensor([data['vdw_hist_y_pbc'] for _, data in g.nodes(data=True)])
        new_dgl_graphs.append(dgl_g)

# Convert list of DGL graphs into a single batched graph
new_batched_graph = dgl.batch(new_dgl_graphs)

# Extract node features for all new graphs

# Pass the batched graph and the node features to the model to get the node embeddings

# Average the node embeddings across nodes to get the logits
new_logits = dgl.mean_nodes(new_batched_graph, 'h')

# The logits are the model's predictions for the new graphs
predictions = new_logits.detach().numpy()
