title: MOFography
text: A powerful python package for the analysis, visualization, featurization, and machine learning on crystalline nanopores. 😀

title: MOFography
text:
The big picture 🖼️
Most of the state-of-the-art approaches to computational materials discovery of MOFs via machine learning (ML), can be summarized in terms of three key components,



A big picture overview of automated discovery of MOFs for any application



Representation: A way to represent the phase space of MOFs. (e.g., atoms and bonds, a periodic graph, a list of strigs representing topology, building blocks and functional groups etc.),
Prediction: Some way to make predictions (a regression model, a data lookup table etc.), and
Optimization/Screening: Some way to select/optimize materials to maximize the desired property(s) (gradient descent, genetic algorithms, Bayes optimization etc.).

title: MOFography
text:
Why MOFography? 🤔



The issues with the current representations of crystalline materials for adsorption


How we represent materials plays a key-role in all these steps. In adsorption, the shape, size, and connectivity of the cavities often play a bigger role than the chemistry of the individual structural building blocks (SBUs) that make up the MOF. Arriving at numerical features that capture the 3D confining environment of a nanoporous materials remains a challenging task till date. Ideally, a good representation should have certain qualities, such as:

Comprehensive: Capture all the relevant information about the
Interpretable: Easy to understand and interpret.
Flexible: Adaptable to different applications of MOFs involving adsorption.

Compact: Easy to store and retrieve, without being too cumbersome.

So, we set out to create one such represention for crystalline nanopores pore graphs or Region Adjacency Graphs (RAGs) that meet at least some of the above criteria for characterization and prediction in adsoption applications.

title: MOFography
text:
The Core Workflow 🚀



The core mofography workflow for constructing pore graphs illustrated using HKUST-1 Metal-Organic Framework


We present a novel approach using advanced image processing techniques to represent the cavities of a material as a pore graph, where the nodes represent regions of arbitrary shape segmented around the local distance maxima, and edges represent the connectivity of these regions. Regions connect through one or more pore windows. As an example,
These nodes and edges can then be annotated with properties relevant to adsorption or pore characterization, which are then aggregated to create MOF-level features. Thus, the pore graph allows us to retain relevant information, without having to work with large 3D images of MOF cavities. Using pore graphs, we can understand and represent MOF pores comprehensively, compare the cavities of two MOFs towards unsupervised ML (E.g., clustering of MOFs), regress pore-influenced properties such as adsorption uptake (supervised ML) and identify key pore characteristics necessary for achieving specific separations.

title: MOFography
text:
Functionality Overview 📚











MOFography (mgr) is feature packed, where you can automatically do a lot more.






Tip



This is not a comprehensive list, please refer to the expanding list of tutorials on the Learn page and API docs on the Reference page for more information.


Just with the core workflow, you can:

Compute distance / LJ energy grids (in parallel or GPU) Segment empty space into individual pockets (cages or - sections along channels and what not)
Compute the connections between these pockets Account for PBC correctly, so you don’t have to work with supercells
Detect pocket connectivity and pore windows (both internal and periodic)
Construct a ‘pore graph’

And because what you end up with is a Networkx graph, you can annotate whatever property you want on it without having to store grids. So now with that possibility, the applications featured in the original paper are:

Detect percolation paths on the graph using path finding. so that gives you PLD, pocket accessibility and stuff like that
Node clustering tasks using some simple geometric or energy features, which tells the different types of pockets in the material
*Shape matching molecules to pockets: Given a rigid molecule how can you quickly find a pocket that matches in LJ shape from a large database like CoRE or IZA. Under the hood it uses energy minimization w/ Bayesian Optimization to do this.

And there is a lot of other useful things: - Visualize framework and pores interactively in Jupyter notebook using (Plotly) and overlay as toggleable layers.






Note



The structure visualization currently is not that advanced, but I am hoping people will contribute in the future. As of now it is good enough for paper figures and TOC images, etc.



Pull large amounts of data from MOFDB asynchronously Geared towards high throughput: Apply any or all of the above functionality in parallel using Dask on HPC

title: MOFography
text:
Our Software Goals 🎯

One stop shop for analysis, features, computing and visualization for you materials
Pure python, so it plays well with your other favorite libraries like ASE, Pymatgen, RDKit etc.
Very easy to extend. If something you need is not there, you should be able to add functionality to it, without worrying too much about nesting, inheritance and all that. In fact, we would encourage you to do exactly that and fine-tune it to your needs. We hope that the code organization is sensible.
To create a community around this package, where users can share their issues, and contribute to the codebase, perhaps to applications that we have not thought of yet.

title: Pockets and paths in IRMOF-1
text: In this example, we analyse the cavities of IRMOF-1, to identify the different types of pockets present using the characteristic geometric size distribution. Further, we represent these properties and connectivity of these pockets as a pore graph, and detect all the paths that run along the length of the unit cell in any direction. The paths are then separated into 1D vs higher dimensional, and compared amongst each other, for uniqueness. Paths are isomorphic only if they connect same types of regions in the same order.

title: Pockets and paths in IRMOF-1
text:
Read the cif file
As usual we read in the framework configuration use ASE, although we are using a CIF file in this example, any format supported by ASE should work.

We then update the ase atoms object covalent bonds

The last two steps are optional, but are quite useful for generating more sensible visualizations of the framework.

title: Pockets and paths in IRMOF-1
text:
Compute PBC
We represmt the Periodic Boudnary Conditions in two differnet ways: 1. As groups of regions that are one and the same in the context of PBC
In this case, for example, all 8 regions on the corners form one group, all 4 regions on the edges parallel to say, the y axis form a group, 2 regions that lie on opposing faces form a periodic group. In IRMOF-1 where the unit cell cuts through the cavities in a symmetric way, each group when put together forms a complete cage.

As a dictionary mapping from old region indices to PBC group index

This contains exactly the same informaton as before, but, provides a convenient way of applying PBC to large numpy arrays.

#region #* Useful PBC information in groups and as mapping
pbc_groups = mgr.get_periodic_map(regions=regions, maxima=maxima, ase_atoms=mat_atoms, maxima_radii=grid.compute()[tuple(maxima.T)], return_conn=True, wall_thickness=4)
pmap= mgr.get_periodic_map(regions=regions, maxima=maxima, ase_atoms=mat_atoms, maxima_radii=grid.compute()[tuple(maxima.T)], return_conn=False, wall_thickness=4)

title: Pockets and paths in IRMOF-1
text:
Find Paths
We find all the paths in the material, that run along the whole lenght of the unit cell, regardless of any particular direction
Note 1: Only the shortest path between a pair of nodes is considered, as there probably a large number of circuitous paths between a pair of nodes in each graph.

Note 2: If two paths are of the exact same length, only one of them is shown, since these paths are often symmetric. You can use networkx to find all the paths between two nodes using find_shortest_paths function.
We then separate the paths out into 1D and higher dimensional using PCA, as 1D paths are perhaps more interesting for practical purposes.
Note 3: 1D path does not refer to teh connectivity of the pockets, it simply means all the region maxima that form the path lie on a fairly straight line, as set by the pca threshold of the leading principal direction

#region #* Let's find the unique 1D and 2D channels in the MOF
pca_list, paths_list= mgr.find_paths(regions, rag2)

# * separate into 1D and 2D paths
threshold = 0.99 #* This is our strict criterio for something to be 1D
paths1d_to_plot = np.array(paths_list)[np.where([check[0]>threshold for check in pca_list])[0]].tolist()
pathshd_to_plot = np.array(paths_list)[np.where([check[0]<threshold for check in pca_list])[0]].tolist()
#
checks1d= np.array(pca_list)[np.where([check[0]>threshold for check in pca_list])[0]].tolist()
checkshd   = np.array(pca_list)[np.where([check[0]<threshold for check in pca_list])[0]].tolist()
#endregion

title: Download a subset from MOFDB and Quick Cluster
text:
In this tutorial, we see how to download a subset of structures from the MOFDB database using a wrapper function in mofography. MOFDB is a large database of nanoporous materials, including MOFs and zeolites that is hosted by Northwestern University. https://mof.tech.northwestern.edu/
For a lot of the materials workflows, it is very convenient to have a subset of structures to be used as a starting point, and to be saved as a pandas dataframe, that some of the textural properties of the material along with its crystallographic information. However, downloading large datasets can be cumbersome. Hence, mofography provides a wrapper that can do this asynchronously, meaning, the pages and pages of your search results will be downloaded in parallel, saving a lot of time. Note that at the time of writing, MOFDB itself has a python API that does this, https://github.com/n8ta/mofdb-client, the comparison of speeds of the two codes is not tested, but you are welcome to test it out as well.
Note that in order to avoid excessive strain on the MOFDB website, it is recommended you save the downloaded dataset locally (we will show this at the end) instead of downloading it every time.
Once we have the dataset, we can create ASE atoms objects from it, pick one or more at random and perform a mofography workflo. In this example, we simply perform the quick cluster workflow, but feel free to build one of your own. If you don’t remember what the Quick Cluster workflow does, please go check out the Quick Cluster notebook in the tutorials.

title: Quick Structure Visualization:
text:
This tutorial shows how to visualize the atoms and bonds in a strucutre

Although mofography is not meant to be a visualization tool, it can be quite handy for visualizing exactly what you want to show using a Plotly backend.
It can be used in a jupyter notebook or in python scripts and turned into interactive html plots of the structure to share with your collaborators.
mofography includes routines to visualize outputs of the RASPA simulation code, we will explore some of that as well.
Note: Although not a prerequisite, checking out the Basic Structure Operations tutorial would be handy in making the most out this tutorial.

title: Quick Structure Visualization:
section: General theme of plotting in mofography
text:
General theme of plotting in mofography
This is the plotting workflow in mofography: - Initialize a Plotly figure - Make the plotting traces using some functions in mofography. Unless specified, mofography functions always return a trace, and not a figure object. We think that this adds more flexibility to the plotting process. - Add the traces to the figure object, along with any of your other traces. - Modify the styling of the figure: You will probably be using Plotly for that, which is infinitely customizable. In some cases there are some handy layouts provided in mofography for shortcuts, as we will see later. - show the figure in a browser or your notebook or save it as an html or image file.
I highly recommend checking out the Plotly documentation for more information on how to customize your plots, which is here: https://plotly.com/python/
and the mofography API documentation to find all the additional options within the plotting functions that may only be glossed over here

Tips and tricks #1:
All the framework traces in mofography (atoms, bonds etc.) are actually 3D meshes (spheres, cylinders etc.) that are built on a Trimesh backend. Hence while they look good, can be a bit taxing on the CPU/GPU. Hence, you may want to play with the resolution of the meshes, perhaps keep it low for quick visualizations and then increase it for publication quality figures.

Quick visualization
Let’s compute the covalent bonds in the structure and turn it into a mesh quickly using a built-in function.

import mofography as mgr 
mat_updated = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(mat_atoms)
frame_mesh = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated)

Finally, let’s visualize the structure using Plotly.

import plotly.graph_objects as go
fig = go.Figure(data=[*frame_mesh])

Tips and tricks #2:
Note the little * in front of the frame_mesh object in figure initalization line? the plot_framework_as_mesh routines returns a list of traces, namely the atoms and bonds. We are simply unpacking the list into separate variables here. If you forget that little * you will get an error.
Although this looks fine, we might want to remove the annoying background and make it look pure white or dark. You can do this easily using Plotly’s layout options. However, mofography provides a couple of preset layouts for quick use.
Let’s try the white layout first,

fig.update(layout=mgr.white_layout).show()

                                                


and now the dark layout,

fig.update(layout=mgr.dark_layout).show()

                                                


note that we haven’t shown the unit cell here, but you can easily add it using the plot_cell function.

fig.add_trace(mgr.plot_cell(mat_updated)).show()

title: egrid_from_atoms2
text:
compute.egrid_from_atoms2(ase_atoms, spacing=0.5, blocksize=20000, forcefield_mixed=None, cutoff=12.5, probe_symbol='He', return_ncells=False, precompute=True)

It takes an ASE atoms object, and returns a dask array of the vdw energy on a grid.

The function is a bit long, but it’s not too complicated.
The first part of the function is just to get the grid points.
The second part is to get the forcefield parameters for the atoms.
The third part is to get the positions of the atoms in the unit cell, and to get the unit cell vectors.
The fourth part is to repeat the unit cell to get the positions of the atoms in the repeated unit cell.
The fifth part is to map the grid point energy function onto the grid points.
The sixth part is to reshape the grid points into a 3D array.
The seventh part is to return the grid points.
The eighth part is to return the number of repetitions of the unit cell if that return_ncells parameter is turned on.











Name
Type
Description
Default




ase_atoms

an ase atoms object
required


spacing

the spacing of the grid points
0.5


blocksize

the size of the chunks that the grid is split into. This is important for memory management, defaults to 20000 (optional)
20000


forcefield_mixed

This is a list of the forcefield parameters for each atom in the unit cell
None


cutoff

the cutoff distance for the Lennard-Jones potential
12.5


probe_symbol

the symbol of the probe atom used to calculate the van der Waals radii, defaults to He (optional)
'He'


return_ncells

if True, returns the number of cells needed to meet the cutoff, defaults to False (optional)
False


precompute

if True, then the AABB is precomputed and passed to the function. If False, then the positions and cell are passed to the function, defaults to True (optional)
True













Type
Description





The grid2 is a dask array, which is a lazy array. It is not computed until you call compute() on it.

title: find_cycles_in_sgraph
text:
analyze.find_cycles_in_sgraph(sgraph, default_ring_sizes=[5, 6, 7, 8, 9])

The function takes a graph and returns a list of cycles in the graph.

The function is written in Python and uses the NetworkX library.
The function takes two arguments:

sgraph: The graph to be analyzed.
default_ring_sizes: A list of integers that specify the sizes of rings to be considered.

The function returns a list of cycles in the graph.
The function first finds all the cycles in the graph using the cycle_basis function from NetworkX.
The function then filters the cycles based on the default_ring_sizes argument.
The function then finds the bond types of the edges in the cycles.
The function then finds the unique cycles in the graph using the find_unique_cycles function

title: rag_from_connections
text:
compute.rag_from_connections(connections, maxima, only_use_internal=True)
This Python function creates a graph representation of regions of interest based on connections and maximum values, with an option to include only internal connections.











Name
Type
Description
Default




connections

Connections is a list of tuples where each tuple contains information about a connection. Each tuple has the following format: (node_id, is_connected, connection_type)
required


maxima

The maxima parameter in the rag_from_connections function seems to represent a list of nodes or regions in a graph. It is used to determine the number of nodes in the graph created by the function. Each element in maxima likely corresponds to a node in the graph
required


only_use_internal

The only_use_internal parameter in the rag_from_connections function is a boolean parameter that determines whether only internal connections should be used when creating the graph. If only_use_internal is set to True, only connections with the type ‘internal’ will be added to the graph, defaults to True (optional)
True













Type
Description





The function rag_from_connections is returning a NetworkX graph G that is constructed based on the input connections, maxima, and the optional parameter only_use_internal. The graph G is built by adding nodes and edges from the input connections based on certain conditions. The nodes of the graph have a ‘labels’ attribute assigned to them.

title: update_with_covalent_bonds
text:
analyze.update_with_covalent_bonds(ase_atoms, nlist=None)
It takes an ASE atoms object and returns an ASE atoms object with the covalent bonds and bond orders added to the info dictionary.
The function also takes an optional argument, nlist, which is a list of nearest neighbors. If nlist is not provided, the function will calculate the nearest neighbors using the voronoi_on_atoms function.
The function uses the pymatgen CovalentBond class to determine if two atoms are bonded. The CovalentBond class uses the bond length and bond tolerance to determine if two atoms are bonded. The bond length is the sum of the covalent radii of the two atoms. The bond tolerance is a user defined parameter. The default value is 0.1.
The function also checks if the nearest image of an atom is in the unit cell. If not, the function will add that site to the structure even if it is across

Type
Description
Default




ase_atoms

the atoms object you want to update
required

a list of pairs of atoms that are neighbors. If you don’t have this, you can use the voronoi_on_atoms function to get it

title: Region Segmenation
text:
In this tutorial we will break down the void space in a material into segmented pockets centered around the local maxima. Hence, the key steps in the tutorial are: - Compute the distance grid - Detect the local maxima in the distance grid - Decide a mask thickness, to distinguish between the void space and the material - Segment the void space into regions - The key parameters that you can tune - Visualize the segmentation results
We have already seen how to compute the distance grid in the Distance grid notebook. If that seems unclear, please go through that tutorial first. We will quickly go through the steps up until the calculation of the distance grid.

title: Region Segmenation

title: Region Segmenation
text:
Compute the distance grid
Let’s compute a distance grid, as we’ve seen before. We are using a pretty coarse grid spacing of 0.5 \(\AA\) here, but you can use a finer grid if you’d prefer that.

dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms(mat_updated, spacing=0.5)

title: Region Segmenation
text:
Watershed segmentation
Under the hood, mofography uses ‘Watershed segmentation’ as implemented in Scikit-Image, to segment the void space into regions. The idea is to use the distance grid to find the local maxima, and then use the watershed algorithm to segment the void space into regions. The watershed algorithm is a pretty powerful tool, and you can read more about it here.
Note that we are working with 3D instead of a 2D image here. The result of watershed segmentation is another 3D grid, where the value at each voxel represents the region number to which the voxel belongs to. The region number of zero is reserved for the background. mask_thickenss:Essentially, by setting a value here we say that all the voxels within a certain mask_thickness of the framework surface are part of the material, and the rest are part of the void space. We do not want to create fictitious holes in the material, like for example, through the metallic nodes in a MOFs or through the center of an cyclic aliphatic or aromatic ring. Hence, a mask_thickness of 1.5 \(\AA\) is a good choice for a lot of the cases.
Let’s do some region segmenation

regions, maxima= mgr.regions_from_dgrid(dgrid.compute(), mask_thickness=1.5)

c:\Users\Arun Gopalan\OneDrive - The University of Manchester\my_cloned_repos\mofography\mofography\compute.py:327: UserWarning: Some maxima excluded as they fell inside the mask_thickness
  warnings.warn('Some maxima excluded as they fell inside the mask_thickness')

title: Region Segmenation
text:
Tunable parameters
As mentioned earlier, there are 2 steps withing the `regions_from_dgrid’ routine in mofography, - Computing the local maxima - Computing the region segmentation.
*h parameter*:
mofography uses the `h_maxima` function from Scikit-Image to compute the local maxima. The `h_maxima` function takes a `h` parameter, which is the minumum height of the maxima. The `h` parameter is set to 0.2 $\AA$ by default. You can change this parameter by passing a different value to the `h_maxima` function. Note that this value is over and above the `mask_thickness` we set earlier. If you are using a coarser grid, you might want to increase this value to avoid fictious maxima occuring from the noise in the distance grid. 
you can read a bit more about it here: https://scikit-image.org/docs/stable/api/skimage.morphology.html#skimage.morphology.h_maxima

*compactness*: This has to do with the uniformity of the watershed segmentation. By default this is set to 0. Scikit image switches from regular watershed to a compact watershed if the compactness parameter is not zero. This parameter is better left untouched. You can read a bit more about it here: https://scikit-image.org/docs/stable/auto_examples/segmentation/plot_compact_watershed.html

title: Region Segmenation
text:
Visualize the segmentation results
As we’ve seen earlier in the Distance grid tutorial, plotting 3D volume data can be cumbersome. Instead, we use distance isosurfaces (like before) to visualize the 3D data, except, that instead of coloring the isosurface by a constant color, we color it by the region number. This way, we can see the different regions on the iso-surface, which serves as proxy for the 3D pore surface.

import plotly.graph_objects as go 
import plotly.express as px 

cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Plotly

isosurface_trace = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid.compute(), isovalue=2.5, ase_atoms=mat_updated, region_labels=regions, cscale=cscale, opacity=0.6)
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_updated)
frame_trace = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated)
